title: Gym chain buys a nutrition firm
prompt: Your client is a premium chain of gyms operating across India. It is considering acquiring a nutrition-focused food manufacturer and retailer that offers pre-cooked and semi-cooked meals. The client believes there are synergies in this acquisition. Should it go ahead? Why or why not?

facts.reveal: The client operates only in India.
The gyms are premium and cater largely to high-income customers.

facts.asks: Target's place in the value chain
facts.reveal: It manufactures and retails nutrition-focused food products, mainly pre-cooked and semi-cooked meals.
You can assume the industry is growing and there is no immediate competitive threat.

facts.asks: After the candidate covers cost synergies
facts.reveal: Where do you see the bigger upside: cost or revenue?
Would expansion into new geographies be part of the synergy story?
How are these financial synergies different from cost synergies?
And how does this translate into valuation?
What execution risks could prevent value capture?

outOfScope: Revenue or EBITDA of either firm

crux.statement: The deal rests on revenue synergies from a captive, high-income, health-conscious member base: meal subscriptions upsold to members, gym-plus-nutrition bundles that lift retention and lifetime value, nutrition outlets as an acquisition channel for gyms, and in-gym counters or cafés. Cost synergies (no capex to build kitchens, shared finance, HR and procurement, raw-material bargaining) are secondary.
crux.clue: "Where do you see the bigger upside: cost or revenue?"
crux.test: Remove "premium gyms, high-income customers" and the cross-sell thesis loses its base. Remove "no immediate competitive threat" and the candidate has to defend the market first.

paths: Three layers: operating synergies (cost, then revenue) → financial synergies (cost of capital) → valuation impact → go or no-go
Strategic fit first, reaching the same three layers

wrongTurns.text: Anchoring the thesis on new geographies (opening gyms is capital-heavy; the source treats it as secondary)
Treating financial synergies as cost synergies
A synergy list with no ranking

answerKey: Financial synergies leave operations alone: more stable, diversified cash flows lower the cost of debt and, over time, the cost of equity
Valuation: higher, steadier cash flows plus a lower cost of capital raise enterprise value; an integrated wellness platform can support a higher multiple
Execution risks: poor in-gym integration, weak cross-selling by staff, wrong pricing or bundling
Mitigations: phased rollout, staff training, pilot bundles, a clear owner for synergy capture

close.condition: The candidate has ranked the synergies and given a go or no-go.

anchors.s5: A generic synergy list with no ranking and no recommendation.
anchors.s7: Ranks revenue over cost with reasons and gives a go or no-go.
anchors.s9: Ties every synergy to the captive member base, separates the operating, financial and valuation layers, and gives conditions and risks with the recommendation.

verifierFlags.text: No numbers in the source: add a member count and attach rate to size the revenue synergy?
verifierFlags.decision: No. Nothing is added without a source; the case stays qualitative and the quantitative dimension is not assessed.

verifierFlags.text: The interviewer reveals very little; most of the content is the candidate's thesis.
verifierFlags.decision: Kept as a full case driven by the five probes. Confidence stays medium.
